**The before-and-after is stark.** In 1959, most Cubans were poor, rural, and Black or mixed-race — precisely the people Batista's Cuba had abandoned. Rural illiteracy ran above 40%. Most campesinos had no access to a doctor, electricity, or running water. Afro-Cubans were formally segregated from beaches, hotels, and jobs. Land and sugar wealth were concentrated in a small elite and US corporations. Havana's glittering averages — which made pre-revolution Cuba look "advanced" on paper — masked this deprivation.

After the revolution:

- Literacy: from roughly 75–80% to 99.8%, verified by UNESCO
- Infant mortality: from roughly 30–40 per 1,000 to around 4–5 today — lower than the United States
- Life expectancy: from the low 60s to about 78–79, comparable to wealthy nations
- Universal free healthcare and education through university, with one of the world's highest doctor-to-patient ratios
- The formal dismantling of segregation and the plantation labor system

These aren't propaganda figures — UN and World Bank data broadly confirm them. For the poor majority and their descendants, this is unambiguously better: they can read, they see doctors, their children survive infancy, and they live nearly twenty years longer.

**Now the honest costs.** The revolution destroyed political freedom — one-party rule, censorship, prisoners of conscience. It never delivered prosperity: wages hover around $30–50 a month, shortages are chronic, the 1990s Special Period brought real hunger, and today's blackouts and the largest exodus in Cuban history show the system failing even on its own terms. Over a million people have left. Some US embargo blame is fair, but socialist economic mismanagement is real too.

**The strongest counterargument** is the counterfactual: Costa Rica achieved comparable health and literacy gains through democracy, suggesting Cuba didn't need dictatorship to get there. That's a fair point — but it's speculative. We know what actually happened, and what actually happened is that the poor majority gained literacy, health, and decades of life.

So my position: yes, most Cubans — the rural and Afro-Cuban majority who made up the actual population of 1959 — live longer, healthier, more educated lives because of the revolution. What they didn't get, and deserved, was freedom and prosperity alongside it.

Yes — for most Cubans alive in 1959, life improved dramatically on the fundamentals, and the gains were real. But the improvement came with steep costs that shouldn't be minimized.

The costs were also real and severe. Cuba became a one-party state with censorship, political prisoners, and no free elections. And comparable countries like Costa Rica achieved similar health and education outcomes through democracy, with far higher living standards — so the revolution was not the only path to those gains.

Verdict: for the landless campesino of 1961, yes, life improved. For most Cubans, measured across the full arc to today, no — poorer, less free, and leaving when they can.

Cuba in 1958 was one of the richest societies in Latin America; today state salaries run a few tens of dollars a month, the ration card introduced in 1962 as a "temporary" measure still exists, housing stock crumbles, and the economy runs on tourism, remittances, and handouts. Politically, Cubans traded one dictatorship for a permanent one-party state with censorship and prisoners of conscience.
